week_beats.diagnose: You see that the loop of trying and failing has trained your mind to expect failure before it even begins.
week_beats.steady: You hold that the same mind that built the apps can be trained to build the next one, step by step.

understanding.core_struggle: A working parent and carer has been building apps for years without success, and now feels stuck, unsure, and like a failure.
understanding.mirror: You give the day everything, then the night goes to the app, and the morning comes with no answer.
understanding.insight: It isn't the apps that have failed you. It's the loop of trying and failing without a clear next step, which has trained your mind to expect failure before it even begins.

verse.speaker: Arjuna
verse.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse.sanskrit: चञ्चलं हि मनः कृष्ण प्रमाथि बलवद्दृढम् । तस्याहं निग्रहं मन्ये वायोरिव सुदुष्करम् ॥
verse.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.
verse.why: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

prasang.title: Mastering the mind
prasang.summary: Arjuna says the mind is restless, stormy and stubborn. Krishna agrees, and says practice and letting go can train it.
prasang.lesson: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

verse.meaning: Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, and as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna agrees, and says that practice and letting go can train it. This is the first time Arjuna admits the struggle out loud. The verse proposes that the mind is naturally hard to control, but it can be trained through steady practice and release. It gently turns toward the life of someone who has been trying for years and now feels the weight of that effort.
verse.for_you: You have been building apps for years without a clear result. The quiet sense of failure is real, and it is not a verdict on your worth. It is simply the mind, restless and stubborn, caught in a loop of trying and not starting.

verse.speaker: Vidula
verse.setting: Queen Vidula rouses her son Sanjaya, who lies defeated and despairing after losing his kingdom.
verse.sanskrit: सर्वेषां कर्मणां तात फले नित्यमनित्यता / अनित्यमिति जानन्तो न भवन्ति भवन्ति च अथ ये नैव कुर्वन्ति नैव जातु भवन्ति ते / ऐकगुण्यमनीहायामभावः कर्मणां फलम्
verse.line: Every result is uncertain. Some who try succeed and some don't. Those who never try never do.
verse.translation: The result of every action is uncertain. Knowing this, some people act and succeed, some do not. But those who never act never succeed at all.
verse.why: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

prasang.title: Vidula rouses her defeated son
prasang.summary: Kunti sends Yudhishthira the old story of Queen Vidula, who finds her son lying defeated after losing his kingdom. She shames, then reasons, then encourages him until he rises and fights for it again.
prasang.story_hook: A prince lay in bed after losing everything, until his mother walked in and refused to let him stay there.
prasang.lesson: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

verse.meaning: Vidula finds her son Sanjaya lying defeated after he has lost his kingdom. She tells him that the result of any action is uncertain, some who try succeed and some do not, but those who never try never do. She is telling him that his past loss does not lock in his future, and that the only way to fail completely is to stop acting.
verse.for_you: You have been building apps for years. Some have failed, but you have not stopped. That means you are still in the trying, and that is the only place success can begin.

verse.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
verse.speaker: Draupadi
verse.setting: Draupadi argues that waiting on fate is no plan: people must act.
verse.sanskrit: कुर्वतो नार्थसिद्धिर्मे भवतीति ह भारत / निर्वेदो नात्र गन्तव्यो द्वावन्तौ यस्य कर्मणः
verse.line: Don't despair because effort hasn't paid off yet. Every attempt can go either way.
verse.translation: 'I keep working and still don't succeed' is no reason to despair. Every effort can end two ways, in success or not; only by not acting is the outcome certain.
verse.why: Do right for its own sake, then work as if it all depends on you.

prasang.title: Do right without reward, and keep working
prasang.summary: Draupadi questions a world where the good suffer; Yudhishthira answers that he does right because it is right, not for reward. Draupadi replies that effort still matters: fate rewards no one who waits.
prasang.lesson: Do right for its own sake, then work as if it all depends on you.

verse.meaning: In the forest, Yudhishthira has stopped trying to reclaim what was lost. He waits for time to heal his grief. Draupadi, his wife, will not let him. She tells him that sitting still is not a choice. It is a surrender. She says that every attempt can end two ways. It can succeed, or it can not. But the one thing that is certain is what happens to those who do nothing. She is telling him that waiting on the world to fix itself is not a plan.
verse.for_you: The same mind that has been trying and failing can be trained to try again, one clear step at a time. Your next move does not have to be a finished app. It can be a single line of code, or a single hour set aside to think about the next one.

verse.speaker: Narrator
verse.setting: Angad plants his foot in Ravana's court and dares anyone to move it; no one can.
verse.sanskrit: भूमि न छाँड़त कपि चरन देखत रिपु मद भाग। कोटि बिघ्न ते संत कर मन जिमि नीति न त्याग ॥
verse.line: A good mind doesn't leave what is right, though a million obstacles come.
verse.translation: The monkey's foot would not leave the ground, and seeing it, the enemy's pride drained away; just as a good person's mind does not abandon what is right, though a million obstacles come.
verse.why: Under insult, keep your purpose; a steady mind does not leave what is right.

prasang.title: Angad in Ravana's court
prasang.summary: Ram sends Angad as envoy, asking him to speak so the work gets done and it does Ravana good too. In court Ravana insults Angad, his dead father and his lord. Angad bears it, remembering that a lion gains no glory by killing a jackal. At last he plants his foot and dares anyone to move it; no warrior can.
prasang.story_hook: Angad sat down in the enemy's court, and they began to insult his father.
prasang.lesson: Under insult, keep your purpose; a steady mind does not leave what is right.

verse.meaning: In the court of Ravana, Angad stands before the king and his warriors and plants his foot on the floor. He dares them to move it. No one can. The narrator sees this and says that a good mind does not leave what is right, though a million obstacles come.
verse.for_you: You have planted your foot too, by keeping at the apps for years. The mind that stays in place against every obstacle is the one that will build the next one, step by step. Hold that purpose.

verse.speaker: Vidura
verse.setting: Vidura counsels the sleepless King Dhritarashtra the night before the peace talks.
verse.sanskrit: निश्चित्य यः प्रक्रमते नान्तर्वसति कर्मणः / अवन्ध्यकालो वश्यात्मा स वै पण्डित उच्यते
verse.line: Decide, then begin. Don't stall halfway, don't waste time, and keep yourself steady.
verse.translation: One who begins only after deciding, does not stop halfway through the work, does not waste time and keeps himself in hand, is called wise.
verse.why: Decide calmly, act steadily, forgive freely, and know what real happiness is made of.

prasang.title: Vidura Niti: the wise and the fool
prasang.summary: Sleepless before the peace talks, King Dhritarashtra calls his half-brother Vidura for counsel. Vidura describes the marks of the wise and the fool, the faults that block progress, and the six joys of life.
prasang.lesson: Decide calmly, act steadily, forgive freely, and know what real happiness is made of.

verse.meaning: King Dhritarashtra cannot sleep the night before the peace talks. He calls his half-brother Vidura. Vidura tells him about the wise person. The wise one decides first. Then they begin the work. They do not stop halfway through. They do not waste time. They keep their mind steady. This is how a person acts with true understanding.
verse.for_you: You have been waiting to feel ready before you build again. Today, put the waiting aside. Pick one small part of your app. Write one line of code. Do this one thing now.

verse.speaker: Angada
verse.setting: The monkeys searching for Sita are exhausted and failing; young Angada rallies them.
verse.sanskrit: अवश्यं कुर्वतां तस्य दृश्यते कर्मणः फलम्। परं निर्वेदमागम्य नहि नोन्मीलनं क्षमम्॥
verse.line: Keep working and the results will come. Sink into despair and it is hard to get back up.
verse.translation: Those who keep working surely see the fruit of their work. But once you sink into deep despair, you cannot rise again.
verse.why: Missing a deadline feels final; it rarely is.

prasang.title: The missed deadline
prasang.summary: The southern search party loses time in a magic cave and misses Sugriva's deadline. Angada rallies them once, then despairs, fearing punishment and certain he will be blamed. Hanuman reasons with him to return.
prasang.story_hook: They came out of the cave to find that spring had already come, and their deadline had gone.
prasang.lesson: Missing a deadline feels final; it rarely is.

verse.meaning: Angada, the young monkey prince, speaks to the tired search party. They have lost the deadline and are sure they will be blamed. Angada tells them that those who keep working will see the results. But if they sink into deep despair, they will not be able to rise again.
verse.for_you: The deadline passed. The apps did not take off. You are tired. This is not the end. Do one small, clear thing today to keep working, before the despair becomes too heavy to lift.

story.title: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind
story.story_hook: One spring morning, a king out for a walk overheard a song that he could not stop thinking about.
story.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. When his doorkeeper calls him to the day's work, he decides not to run away: he gets up and does his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutches.
story.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

anchor.speaker: Janaka
anchor.setting: King Janaka, alone on his palace roof after overhearing wandering sages, rethinks his life.
anchor.sanskrit: संपदश्च विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेच्चित्तेन संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा हन्त मन्ये महापदः ॥ आपदोऽपि विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेन्मनसि संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा मन्ये मनसि संपदः ॥
anchor.line: Good fortune the mind clutches becomes trouble. Trouble the mind accepts becomes a kind of fortune.
anchor.translation: All those dazzling fortunes, if the mind clings to them, are really great calamities in grand disguise. And all those varied misfortunes, if the mind accepts them, are really fortunes.
anchor.why: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.
anchor.misuse: Accepting a hardship doesn't mean not fixing what can be fixed.

script: There is a quiet exhaustion to you right now, the kind that comes from carrying a full day of work, the children, and your parents, and still having the energy to wonder if any of it means something. You are in the middle of your life, and you feel the weight of it.

Arjuna stands in the middle of the battlefield. He has laid down his bow and his arrows. He has fought his own people, his own teachers, and now he cannot fight anymore. He turns to Krishna and admits that his mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. Arjuna said:
चञ्चलं हि मनः कृष्ण प्रमाथि बलवद्दृढम्, तस्याहं निग्रहं मन्ये वायोरिव सुदुष्करम्.
In plain words: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.

Krishna does not tell Arjuna that the mind is easy to control. He agrees that it is hard, like trying to catch the wind. But he says that practice and letting go can train it. This is the truth underneath. The mind is not your enemy. It is simply restless. The problem is not that you have failed. The problem is that you have been trying to force the wind into a shape it does not want to hold.

Today, you do not need to build another app. You only need to notice the wind. When you sit down to work, notice when the mind pulls you toward the past and the future. Do not fight it. Just let it go, and bring it back to the one thing in front of you.
The wind is not the enemy.

depth.life: You sit with your phone after the kids are asleep. You have been building apps for years, and each one failed. You do not know if you are disciplined or just stubborn, and the quiet sense of failure is heavy.
depth.points: Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless and as hard to hold as the wind. This restlessness is not a flaw. It is the nature of the mind, caught in a loop of trying and not starting.
depth.practice: Sit for one minute and let your thoughts move without holding them. Do not try to stop them.
depth.question: What does it feel like to let the mind move without holding it?
